tier_reason: First-party Igalia benchmark with public driver code (pflua-bench bench.lua, bench.mk, results/ping-flood/*.csv) and a stated CPU (i7-3770); the Linux BPF/eBPF JIT shared objects are built with gcc -O3 per their Makefiles, but the main libpcap baseline is the Debian system libpcap with version and build flags unstated and no gcc version is given, so it falls short of A.

corrections.baseline: libpcap's user-space BPF interpreter (pcap_offline_filter in the Debian system libpcap, version and build flags not stated) running bytecode from pcap_compile with libpcap's optimizer on; also the 2011 Linux kernel BPF JIT and the 2014 Linux eBPF JIT (C, built with gcc -O3 as user-space shared objects in pflua-bench), whose filters run as JIT-emitted machine code
corrections.workload: Run pflang (tcpdump filter language) expressions 'accept all', 'ip', 'tcp', 'tcp port 5555' and 'icmp' over a 60-64 MB capture of 961,180 ICMP ping packets ('tcp' and 'tcp port 5555' match none of them), in millions of packets per second (MPPS). One discarded warm-up set, then 20 sets per engine in one process (bench.mk ITERATIONS?=20; the README says 50); each measurement loops over all packets for at least 0.1 s and checks the expected match count. Results committed 2015-02-03.
corrections.claimed_speedup: pflua-bench README conclusion: 'In many circumstances, pflua is the fastest pflang implementation out there, by a long shot.' (the pflua README says 'by a wide margin'). Medians of the 20 runs in results/ping-flood (derived from page data), MPPS pflua vs libpcap vs linux-bpf vs linux-ebpf: 'tcp' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 62.2 vs 56.1; 'tcp port 5555' 89.9 vs 37.9 vs 61.8 vs 57.6; 'icmp' 89.9 vs 54.8 vs 83.5 vs 77.7; 'ip' 91.6 vs 68.0 vs 85.3 vs 78.7; 'accept all' 127.9 vs 92.1 vs 109.8 vs 95.4. About 2.4x libpcap and 1.45x the 2011 Linux BPF JIT on 'tcp'. The bpf-lua engine (libpcap's BPF translated to Lua) gets 88.4 MPPS on 'tcp', within 2% of pflua.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: pflua and bpf-lua: LuaJIT from the pflua submodule built with its default make. linux-bpf-jit and linux-ebpf-jit: gcc -g -Wall -fPIC -O3 (their Makefiles; gcc version not stated). libpcap: Debian system library loaded with ffi.load("pcap"), version and build flags not stated.
corrections.why_faster: README (pflua, Performance section): LuaJIT trace compilation emits machine code specialised to the traffic seen, pflua can hoist and eliminate bounds checks while BPF checks every packet access, it works in network byte order, and it uses LuaJIT's register allocator and optimizer while the kernel JIT's optimizer is limited. The raw data narrow this: bpf-lua (libpcap-optimised BPF compiled to Lua) runs within 2% of pflua, so the gain comes from LuaJIT compiling the filter inline into the benchmark loop's trace rather than from pflua's own optimizer, while libpcap and the Linux JITs are called through the LuaJIT FFI once per packet.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark by the pflua authors; libpcap version and flags and the gcc version are not stated, so tier C. The comparison is LuaJIT-compiled code against a C interpreter (libpcap) and two other runtime JITs (Linux BPF/eBPF), not against AOT-compiled C doing the same work, so it is a weak fit for runtime-jit-beats-aot. Harness asymmetry: pflua and bpf-lua predicates are Lua functions inlined into the LuaJIT trace of the timing loop, while libpcap (pcap_offline_filter, plus a pcap_pkthdr written per packet) and the Linux JITs (run_filter in a .so) are called through the FFI per packet; the 'accept all' row, which does no filtering, already differs (127.9 vs 92.1 vs 109.8 vs 95.4 MPPS). Subtracting the 'accept all' time per packet (derived from page data), the 'tcp' filter costs about 3.3 ns in pflua vs 15.5 ns in libpcap and 7.0 ns in linux-bpf, but the 'icmp' filter costs 3.3 ns in pflua vs 2.9 ns (linux-bpf) and 2.4 ns (linux-ebpf), so pflua's 'icmp' lead over the Linux JITs is call overhead. libpcap runs with its optimizer on (pf/libpcap.lua passes optimize=true), so it is not an unoptimised interpreter. The workload is homogeneous and 'tcp' filters match no packet, which suits a tracing JIT; on the real-world wingolog.org-2 capture pflua is sometimes slower than libpcap and the Linux JITs (README blames LuaJIT trace state-transfer costs). The README prose (about 180 MPPS, 'all results are faster than the accept all loop') does not match the committed CSVs, where 'accept all' is the fastest row for every engine. Results date from 2015-02-03; last commits 2017-01-30 (pflua) and 2016-12-05 (pflua-bench).

notes: Numbers re-derived from the five ping-flood CSVs and match the record (20 runs, not 50). Main shortcomings: first-party, libpcap build unstated, per-packet FFI call overhead favours pflua (its icmp lead over the Linux JITs disappears after subtracting the accept-all loop), win is LuaJIT trace compilation not pflua's optimizer (bpf-lua ties it), weak category fit (JIT vs interpreter and other JITs), 2015 data.

tier_reason: The 0.866 relative time is on the page, but no valid same-work comparison exists: the checked-in VB.NET project (src/visualbasic/vbnet) times the benchmark's own polynomial sine/cosine and arctangent routines while the C reference (src/c/Makefile, INTRIG off) calls the C library's trig functions, and the VB.NET row ran on Windows XP against a C row built with GCC 3.2.3 on Linux, with no CPU, .NET version or C build named for the VB.NET run; under the cross-run and crippled-baseline precedents this is D.

corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the source. The checked-in VB.NET project compiles the #Else branches of modFBENCH.vb (INTRIG is not defined in that file), so the timed loop calls the benchmark's own polynomial fSin/fCos and the rational-approximation aTan behind aSin (fbench_lib.vb), plus System.Math.Tan, Sqrt and one Cos, while the C reference calls libm sin, cos, asin and tan; with different trig work and a different OS on each side, the ratio cannot be attributed to the CLR JIT.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: VB.NET: 'All optimisations', Windows XP; the checked-in fbench.vbproj (Visual Studio .NET project, ProductVersion 7.0.9955, an upgrade-wizard conversion of Jim White's 2005 VB6 port) has a Release config with Optimize=true and RemoveIntegerChecks=true; .NET Framework version not stated; timed with GetTickCount in a WinForms app. C baseline: GCC 3.2.3 -O3 on Linux (src/c/Makefile: gcc -Wall -O3 -lm, INTRIG commented out so libm trig is used).
corrections.caveats: Different work on the two sides: the VB.NET timed loop mostly uses the benchmark's internal polynomial trig routines (the C equivalent is the INTRIG build), while the C reference row uses libm trig; on the page's own Pentium 4 / GCC 3.2.3 -O3 row the C INTRIG build is 0.01074 s vs 0.00862 s for the libm build, so the two modes are not interchangeable. The VB.NET row ran on Windows XP and the C reference row is GCC 3.2.3 on Linux; the page says each language was compared with C 'on the same machine' but names neither the machine nor the C build used for this row. The reference compiler is 2003-vintage (the page's own G++ 5.4.0 -O3 row is 0.939, also faster than the C reference). No mechanism, CPU model, .NET version or date for the VB.NET run is given. The VB6 build of the same port is 1.132 (slower). CC BY-SA 4.0 is not an OSI licence, so reference only. Last commit 2021-09-24 and the author does not say the work is complete.

notes: Numbers on the page match (VB.NET 0.866, VB6 1.132), but the checked-in VB.NET source shows the port runs a different trig implementation from the C reference and on a different OS, so this is not a same-work language comparison; downgraded to D. maintenance_status corrected to abandoned (no completion statement; last commit 2021-09-24).

tier_reason: First-party BenchmarkDotNet table in the README with public benchmark code (src/ZstdSharp.Benchmark/Benchmark.cs), .NET 9.0.7 and an i7-12700 stated, but the native side is a prebuilt libzstd.dll whose compile flags are not recorded, so it falls short of A.

corrections.baseline: Native zstd 1.5.7 (C) called through P/Invoke (ZSTD_compressCCtx / ZSTD_decompressDCtx with reused contexts) from the checked-in prebuilt x64 libzstd.dll, added in the 'Ported zstd v1.5.7' commit of 2025-02-25; its strings list zstd_preSplit.c (new in zstd 1.5.7) and a MinGW-w64 GCC 14.2.0 runtime, but the zstd objects' compile flags are not recorded.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: .NET 9.0.7 RyuJIT, X64 AVX2 (BenchmarkDotNet v0.15.2, .NET SDK 9.0.302). Native libzstd.dll: prebuilt MinGW-w64 x64 binary under src/Zstd.Extern/x64 (zstd 1.5.7; CRT objects built by GCC 14.2.0 with -O2 -march=nocona; flags for the zstd objects themselves not recorded).
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the source. A plausible but unverified cause: RyuJIT compiles for the host CPU (AVX2, BMI and LZCNT/TZCNT) while the native DLL appears to be a generic x86-64 MinGW build; native decompression, where zstd dispatches to BMI2 code at run time, stays faster.
corrections.caveats: The source gives no mechanism for the compression wins, and the result is mixed: ZstdSharp is about 4% and 10% faster at compression levels 1 and 15 but 13% slower at level 5 and 7-12% slower at decompression, the usual hot path. The native baseline is a vendored prebuilt libzstd.dll (zstd 1.5.7 judging by its strings) whose compiler flags are not given, so it may be a generic x86-64 build rather than a host-tuned -O3 build; hence tier C. Benchmark.cs hard-codes level = 1, so the level 5 and 15 rows came from edited code, and the benchmark never checks that the C# compressed output matches native. The README numbers (updated 2025-07-17) predate PR #74 (merged 2026-09-25), which fixed stale or uninitialised useRowMatchFinder/postBlockSplitter values in ZSTD_CCtxParams_init_internal that made output differ from native and compression 2-5x slower when a context was reused across levels; the README benchmark reuses one context at one level, so it is probably unaffected. Native calls go through P/Invoke, a negligible per-call overhead at 5-2,200 ms per call. Only one input file (dickens), first-party run on Windows 10. ZstdSharp is a pure C# port, not a wrapper of the native library.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly. Native DLL identified as zstd 1.5.7 (zstd_preSplit.c in its strings), so baseline version matches the port, but build flags remain unknown. Shortcomings: first-party, native flags unknown, mixed result (slower at level 5 and decompression), no output check, level parameter hard-coded to 1, numbers predate correctness fix PR #74 (probably unaffected).
